sections.b: Leviticus 1–7 names five kinds of offering. The burnt offering (olah, "what goes up") is wholly burned. The grain offering (minchah, "tribute") is flour, oil and incense, mostly eaten by the priests. The peace offering (shelamim) is a shared meal in which God receives the fat, the priest a thigh and breast, and the worshiper the rest. The sin offering (hatta't) purifies the sanctuary after unintended sin and impurity, its blood put on the altar horns or carried inside. The guilt offering (asham) pays for a holy thing misused or a neighbor wronged, with a fifth added (Leviticus 5:14–6:7). Chapters 1–5 speak to the worshiper; 6–7 repeat the list for the priests.
sections.refs: Leviticus 1:1–17; Leviticus 2:1–16; Leviticus 3:1–17; Leviticus 4:1–35; Leviticus 5:14–6:7; Leviticus 7:37–38

sections.b: Theories differ. Sacrifice as gift (E. B. Tylor): the word korban means "what is brought near." As meal and communion (W. Robertson Smith): the peace offering is eaten before God. As purification (Jacob Milgrom): the blood of the sin offering is a "ritual detergent" that cleans the sanctuary, not the sinner. As substitution: the hand leaned on the head (Leviticus 1:4) marks the animal as standing for the worshiper, a reading Milgrom rejects and others (Kiuchi, Sklar, Gane) defend in different forms. Leviticus itself gives one key explanation: "a body's life is in its blood, and I myself have given it to you on the altar, to make atonement for your lives" (Leviticus 17:11).

common: Sacrifices were only for deliberate sins (the sin and guilt offerings covered unintended sins, impurity and some admitted wrongs; defiant sin had no sacrifice, Numbers 15:30).

Sacrifice worked automatically, whatever the worshiper's heart (Leviticus requires confession, Leviticus 5:5, and the Mishnah says the Day of Atonement does not atone for one who sins planning to repent later, Mishnah Yoma 8:9).
uncommon: The poor could bring a tenth of an ephah of flour as a sin offering, the only bloodless one (Leviticus 5:11–13).
Rabbinic tradition held that in the age to come all sacrifices would cease except the thank offering (Leviticus Rabbah 9:7).

sections.b: Leviticus 8 carries out the ordination ordered in Exodus 29: washing, robing, anointing, a bull and two rams, blood on the right ear, thumb and toe, and seven days at the tent's door. On the eighth day Aaron begins and the glory appears (Leviticus 9). The priests' work is summed up in Leviticus 10:10–11: to separate holy from ordinary and unclean from clean, and to teach Israel. Much of chapters 11–15 is a manual for that task: the priest inspects skin and walls and pronounces.
sections.refs: Leviticus 8:1–36; Leviticus 9:1–24; Leviticus 10:8–11; Leviticus 13:1–3; Ezekiel 44:23; Malachi 2:7

sections.b: The priests lived from the altar: most of the grain offerings, the meat of the sin and guilt offerings, and the breast and right thigh of every peace offering (Leviticus 6:14–7:36). These are "most holy" and must be eaten in a holy place. Paul appeals to the same principle for those who preach (1 Corinthians 9:13–14).

uncommon: The high priest's own unintended sin required the same costly bull as a sin of the whole people (Leviticus 4:3, 4:14).

sections.b: Leviticus shows Aaron at his height and his lowest point in three chapters. He is anointed and ordained (chapter 8), offers first for himself and then for the people, and blesses them as the glory appears (chapter 9). That same day his sons Nadab and Abihu die before the LORD, and "Aaron was silent" (Leviticus 10:3). He then answers Moses wisely over the uneaten sin offering (10:19–20). Chapter 16 makes him the one man who may enter the inner room, once a year, with blood.

claude.title: Aaron's silence
claude.body: My own reading: Aaron's silence in Leviticus 10:3 is the first time he does not speak in a crisis. At the golden calf he spoke too much and excused himself (Exodus 32:22–24). Here, faced with God's judgment on his own sons, he says nothing, and later his single question (10:19) is about doing right before God. Leviticus may be showing a priest restored by grief to the humility his office needs.

sections.b: Exodus builds the tabernacle; Leviticus shows it working. God now speaks "from the tent of meeting" (Leviticus 1:1) instead of from the mountain. Its zones govern every law: the courtyard altar where worshipers bring their offerings, the tent where the priests tend the lamp, table and incense, and the inner room entered once a year. Uncleanness among the people pollutes the sanctuary at a distance (Leviticus 15:31), so the purity laws of chapters 11–15 serve one goal: keeping a home fit for God "which stays with them in the middle of their uncleanness" (16:16).

The call first sounds at the end of the food laws (Leviticus 11:44–45) and becomes the motto of chapters 17–26 (19:2; 20:26). In chapters 1–16 holiness is mostly a status of places, things and people set apart for God. It can be graded (holy, most holy), it can be passed on by touch (6:18, 27), and it is dangerous to the careless (10:1–3). Mary Douglas and Philip Jenson describe the system as a map of zones running from the most holy place out to the wilderness. 1 Peter 1:15–16 quotes Leviticus 11:44 to call Christians to a holy life.

common: Holy and clean mean the same thing (they differ: the ordinary can be clean or unclean; only the clean can become holy, Leviticus 10:10).

sections.b: One goat is "for the LORD," the other "for Azazel" (Leviticus 16:8). Three readings are old. A place: the rabbis read the word as a rough cliff in the wilderness, and the Mishnah says the goat was pushed off a cliff (Yoma 6:6). The goat itself: the Greek and Latin took it as "the goat that goes away," which Tyndale made "scapegoat." A demon or fallen angel: 1 Enoch names Azazel as a rebel angel bound in the desert, and many modern scholars think the name refers to a wilderness spirit, though the rite gives him nothing; the goat only carries sin back to where it belongs. Comparable rites of sending away a carrier animal are known from Hittite and Syrian texts.

The Mishnah tractate Yoma preserves the Second Temple rite; after AD 70 the synagogue replaced it with prayer, the Avodah recital of the high priest's service, and confession. Rabbi Akiva closes Yoma: "Happy are you, Israel! Before whom are you made clean, and who makes you clean? Your Father in heaven" (Mishnah Yoma 8:9). Christians read the chapter through Hebrews 9–10, where Christ enters the true holy place once for all.

common: The scapegoat was sacrificed (it was not; it was sent away alive, Leviticus 16:10, 16:21–22).
The day was only for the people's sins (it also cleansed the sanctuary, tent and altar, Leviticus 16:16–19).
uncommon: In the Mishnah the high priest speaks the divine name aloud in each of his three confessions, and the people fall on their faces and answer "Blessed be the name of his glorious kingdom forever" (Mishnah Yoma 3:8; 4:2; 6:2).

sections.b: Leviticus 9 ends with the glory of the LORD appearing to all the people, and fire coming out "from before the LORD" to eat up the offering (9:23–24). The same fire, in the next verse, eats up Nadab and Abihu (10:2). God's glory both accepts and consumes. Solomon's temple is dedicated the same way (2 Chronicles 7:1–3), and Elijah's sacrifice on Carmel (1 Kings 18:38–39).

Incense is both the means of the sin in Leviticus 10 and a shield in Leviticus 16. Nadab and Abihu bring incense with "strange fire" and die. On the Day of Atonement the high priest must bring coals from the altar and a cloud of incense to cover the atonement lid "so that he does not die" (16:12–13). The Mishnah has the elders make the high priest swear to follow their ruling on the incense (Yoma 1:5); the Talmud explains that Sadducees lit it outside the veil, Pharisees inside (Yoma 19b).

Leviticus calls its units torah, a "procedure" or "instruction": "This is the procedure for the burnt offering" (Leviticus 6:9), "for a person with skin disease" (14:2). Torah here means practical teaching for priests and people before it becomes the name for the whole five books. Traditional Jewish education began children with Leviticus: "Let the pure come and study purity" (Leviticus Rabbah 7:3). The Sifra, the rabbinic commentary on the book, is the foundation of the laws of sacrifice and purity in the Mishnah.

Leviticus names four sources of ritual uncleanness: certain animals and their carcasses (chapter 11), childbirth (12), scale disease in skin, cloth and walls (13–14), and discharges from the sexual organs (15); Numbers 19 adds the corpse. Uncleanness is not sin. It comes from normal life (birth, sex, menstruation, burial), it is often unavoidable, and it is removed by time, washing and, in serious cases, offerings. Its danger is to the sanctuary: "so that they do not die in their uncleanness by making my tabernacle, which is among them, unclean" (Leviticus 15:31).

sections.b: Jacob Milgrom argued that the common thread is death: blood and semen lost, skin wasting, carcasses. Mary Douglas saw a map of order and wholeness. Jonathan Klawans distinguishes this ritual impurity from the moral impurity of grave sins such as idolatry, incest and murder, which defile the land and are not washed off (Leviticus 18:24–28). Hyam Maccoby stressed that ritual impurity is a condition of being close to the holy, not a fault.

Jesus touches the unclean and heals them (Mark 1:40–42; Mark 5:25–34; Mark 5:41). Mark 7 records his teaching that what enters a person cannot defile, which Mark glosses "making all foods clean" (Mark 7:19). Peter's vision in Acts 10 applies the lesson to people: "What God has made clean, you must not call common." Whether these passages abolish the purity laws or relativize them is debated (Furstenberg, Rudolph, Boyarin).

Land animals are clean if they both have a split hoof and chew the cud; water creatures if they have fins and scales; birds unless they are on the list of some twenty forbidden kinds, mostly birds of prey; winged insects only if they have jointed legs for leaping. Touching or carrying a carcass makes a person unclean until evening. Deuteronomy 14 gives a parallel list. The stated reason is holiness: "Be holy, for I am holy" (Leviticus 11:44–45), and in 20:24–26 separation from the nations.

Explanations include hygiene (Maimonides; disputed), symbol and order (Mary Douglas), ethical allegory (Letter of Aristeas, Philo, Barnabas), identity (pork avoidance may appear as an ethnic marker in Iron Age hill villages, though this is debated), reverence for life (Jacob Milgrom: the system limits killing and, with the ban on blood, teaches that life belongs to God), analogy (Gordon Wenham, after Douglas: unclean, clean and altar animals mirror the nations, Israel and the priests), economics and ecology (Marvin Harris), and divine decree (rabbinic chok), obeyed without a reason. Several may be true at once.

Jews kept the laws under persecution (Daniel 1; 2 Maccabees 6–7) and they remain the basis of kashrut. The early church debated them (Galatians 2:11–14; Acts 15), and most Christians follow Mark 7:19 and Romans 14 in treating them as no longer binding, while some (Seventh-day Adventists, many Messianic Jews) keep the clean-animal distinction.

common: The Bible bans pork for health reasons (Leviticus gives no health reason, only holiness and separation, Leviticus 11:44–45; 20:25–26).
The food laws were first given at Sinai (Genesis already distinguishes clean and unclean animals in the flood story, Genesis 7:2).
uncommon: The hyrax and hare do not technically chew the cud; their chewing motion and reingestion of droppings may explain the classification (Leviticus 11:5–6).

sections.b: The Hebrew tsara'at was translated lepra in Greek and "leprosy" in English, and medieval Europe identified it with Hansen's disease. The symptoms in Leviticus 13 do not fit: no numbness or loss of limbs, cases that clear within weeks, and the same word used for mold in cloth and houses (13:47–59; 14:33–53). Most scholars think it named a group of scaly skin conditions, and many translations now use "skin disease" or "scale disease."

The person declared unclean tears his clothes, lets his hair loose, covers his upper lip and calls "Unclean, unclean," living alone outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45–46), the signs of a mourner. When healed, he returns through a two-stage rite: two birds, one killed and one set free (14:4–7), then on the eighth day blood and oil on ear, thumb and toe, as at a priest's ordination (14:14–18). Miriam (Numbers 12), Naaman (2 Kings 5), the four men at Samaria's gate (2 Kings 7) and King Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26) are its best-known sufferers.
sections.refs: Leviticus 13:45–46; Leviticus 14:1–32; Numbers 12:10–15; 2 Kings 5:1–14; 2 Kings 7:3–10; 2 Chronicles 26:19–21

sections.b: Jesus touches a man with skin disease, heals him and sends him to the priest "as evidence for them" (Mark 1:40–44); he heals ten and sends them to the priests (Luke 17:11–19). The rabbis, reading Numbers 12 and Deuteronomy 24:9, tied the disease to slander (Arakhin 16a).

common: Biblical "leprosy" is Hansen's disease (the symptoms do not match, and the word also covers mold in houses and cloth).
uncommon: A person whose whole body turned white was declared clean (Leviticus 13:12–13).

sections.b: Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's two oldest sons, went up the mountain and saw the God of Israel (Exodus 24:1, 9–11). On the day of the tabernacle's inauguration they brought "strange fire" before the LORD, "which he had not commanded them," and fire from the LORD ate them up (Leviticus 10:1–2). They died childless (Numbers 3:4), and the priesthood passed through Eleazar and Ithamar. The Day of Atonement law is dated "after the death of Aaron's two sons" (Leviticus 16:1).
sections.refs: Exodus 6:23; Exodus 24:1; Exodus 24:9–11; Leviticus 10:1–7; Leviticus 16:1; Numbers 3:4; Numbers 26:61; 1 Chronicles 24:2

sections.b: The text gives no motive. Explanations include fire taken from outside the altar (compare 16:12), incense at the wrong time, drunkenness (from 10:9), entering improperly dressed, presumption in deciding a matter before Moses, and desire to succeed him (Sifra; Leviticus Rabbah 20; Eruvin 63a; Sanhedrin 52a). Philo and some midrash read them as holy men who drew too near out of love (Rashi on 10:3).

common: God struck them for a minor slip in procedure (the story puts them at the height of honor, Exodus 24:9–11, and the point is the danger of approaching the holy on one's own terms, Leviticus 10:3).

sections.b: Hebrews reads Leviticus as a "shadow of the good things that were coming" (Hebrews 10:1). The high priest offering first for himself (Leviticus 9:7; 16:6) contrasts with Christ, who needs no offering for himself (Hebrews 7:27). Entry into the inner room once a year with blood (Leviticus 16:2, 14) points to Christ's entry into heaven "once for all" with his own blood (Hebrews 9:7–12). Bodies of sin offerings burned outside the camp (Leviticus 4:12; 16:27) point to Jesus suffering outside the city gate (Hebrews 13:11–13).
sections.refs: Leviticus 4:12; Leviticus 9:7; Leviticus 16:2–17; Leviticus 16:27; Hebrews 7:27; Hebrews 9:7–14; Hebrews 10:1–4; Hebrews 13:11–13

sections.b: The only law of circumcision in Leviticus is a clause in the childbirth law: "On the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin is to be circumcised" (Leviticus 12:3). The rabbis derived from this that circumcision overrides the Sabbath (Shabbat 132a), and Jesus argued from the same practice (John 7:22–23).

Aaron's first sin offering is a calf (Leviticus 9:2, 8), the only calf in the sacrificial laws, and the Sifra links it to the golden calf: Aaron atones with the animal he once made an idol. The people's offering, by contrast, includes a goat, which the Sifra ties to the goat whose blood Joseph's brothers used to deceive their father (Genesis 37:31).

Aaron lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them (Leviticus 9:22); then Moses and Aaron blessed them again (9:23). The words are not given, but the rabbis took them to be the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24–26, still pronounced with raised hands in synagogues. Luke ends his Gospel with Jesus lifting his hands to bless the disciples (Luke 24:50–51).

Seven-day periods run through Leviticus 8–16: the priests' ordination (8:33), a mother after a son (12:2), quarantine for skin disease (13:4–5), waiting after healing (14:8), discharges and periods (15:13, 19, 28). Blood is spattered seven times (4:6; 14:7; 16:14, 19). The eighth day follows as a new start: the priests begin (9:1), a son is circumcised (12:3), the healed come before the LORD (14:10, 23; 15:14, 29).

sections.b: More than a dozen manuscripts of Leviticus were found at Qumran, including several in the old paleo-Hebrew script (1QpaleoLev, 2QpaleoLev, 6QpaleoLev, 11QpaleoLev-a) and two Greek copies (4QLXXLev-a, 4QpapLXXLev-b). They agree closely with the Masoretic Text; most differences are small, sometimes siding with the Samaritan Pentateuch or the Septuagint. 11QpaleoLev-a, published by Freedman and Mathews (1985), is the largest. Leviticus is one of the best-preserved books of the Hebrew Bible.

Leviticus requires confession before certain offerings: "he is to confess the sin he has committed" (Leviticus 5:5), and on the Day of Atonement the high priest confesses all Israel's sins over the goat (16:21). For wrongs against a neighbor the sinner must repay in full, add a fifth, and only then bring his guilt offering (6:1–7). The rabbis drew the principle that the Day of Atonement does not atone for wrongs between people until the injured one is appeased (Mishnah Yoma 8:9), and Maimonides based his laws of repentance on these verses.
